title: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It will be observed that in all these animals the load upon the fore-feet preponderates considerably over that upon the hind, the preponderance being rather greater in the elephant than in the horse, and markedly greater in the camel and the llama than in the other two.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Distribution of load in quadrupeds”. Scope: large terrestrial quadrupedal mammals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a direct quantitative measurement with clear refutation thresholds. Some open biomechanics data exist, but the named large species and standardized standing conditions are not comprehensively covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Calculate forelimb share of total vertical ground-reaction force during quiet stance in large quadrupeds and test the stated species-specific percentages and general forelimb excess.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Force-plate data for elephants, camels and llamas are limited.

Load distribution changes with posture and movement.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.98

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The percentages are precise enough that force-plate data can settle them species by species. An open horse dataset exists and records a dynamic gait, so it speaks to load sharing without matching the standing condition. The other named species have published measurements that would have to be compiled before the full numerical claim can be confirmed or refuted.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sum vertical ground reactions on the forefeet and hindfeet of standing or slowly walking horses, elephants, camels and llamas and express the fore share of body weight. The claim is confirmed if horses and elephants fall near 55-58 percent and camels and llamas near two-thirds; shares near one-half, or a reversed ranking of those species, would refute the stated figures.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The deposited horse series is a ridden gallop, whereas Thompson's percentages are for the standing load distribution.

Elephant, camel and llama force-plate tables are scattered in papers rather than one open archive.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.48
operationalizability: 0.92
discriminating power: 0.74
data existence: 0.58
